pages.titre: How to reach us about a figure or an engagement.
pages.lede: Name the figure you are questioning and where you saw it. Every number here has a source, so we start from the same one. No attachments, except the two named below.
pages.description: A message that names a figure and its source starts a real discussion. Attach no file, except the list for a Screening report or a Routing free-test record.

sections.h2: Two ways to reach us, email and a public issue
html: Write to contact@crusetra.com: the direct channel. For anything worth deciding in the open (a disputed figure, a wrong line, a question others will have), open an issue at github.com/ArslaneSempai-ui/crusetra-routing. An issue is public, so keep confidential material out of it: no client names, no records, no internal figures. Either way, attach no file, except the list you send for a Screening report, or the measured record of a Routing free test. For anything else, a channel for records is opened in the engagement letter, before signature, like every other term.

The page you are on and the figure you dispute: each one here has a declared source, so we can meet at it. If you disagree with a measurement, bring your own rerun. The record is frozen and the command is public, so you can reproduce it. If you measured your own cases, bring the report the tool wrote beside your CSV: it contains rates and their confidence intervals, and no values from your documents.

We receive none of your documents, and we do not want a sample. Two things do reach us by email when you ask for a report: the list of names for a Screening report, and the measured record of a Routing free test, which holds verdicts and counts and no value read from a document. The tool exists so your documents never leave your machine. A sample attached to a public issue is published, and a clone, once made, cannot be taken back. If your question needs your data, the answer is a command that runs where the data lives, and we will point you to it.

Two shortcuts. On a fresh clone, node src/premiere-reponse.mjs prints the conclusion in under a second, with what would flip it. And the eight objections a bank's reviewers actually raise are already answered, mechanism by mechanism, in Appendix C, Questions below.

sections.h2: What this site does to visitors: nothing
html: No cookies, no analytics, no tracking, no forms. The scripts on this site do two things only. The main screen keeps its animation and the browser tab title in step with each other. The appendix pages open their sections when you print. You can switch the scripts off and the site still works. Each number shown here has a stated source, and the file that states each source is public, next to this page: releve.json. Those numbers come from our public test set, a file we froze. A content hash is a code that identifies a file by its contents. The one in the masthead, the band at the top of the page, is the content hash of that frozen file.

The tool publishes a retraction file, which lists each published conclusion that turned out to be wrong, and a test holds that file open. The same applies to this site. When a number here is corrected, the correction is made in the open and the change is recorded.

pages.titre_onglet: OFAC's July 14 shipping sanctions: name variants | Crusetra
pages.titre: Name variants to catch in OFAC's July 14 shipping sanctions
pages.lede: On July 14, 2026, OFAC sanctioned a group of container lines, ship owners and freight firms. If one of these names appears in a file you screen, it may be spelled differently, because shipping papers pass through many hands. Here are the variants we found, and how our screening tool handled them.
pages.description: OFAC's July 14, 2026 shipping sanctions: the name variants in its own documents. Our tool found the right entry as a strong match for 96 of 102 names.

html: That day OFAC added 54 entries to its Specially Designated Nationals List (SDN List), covering 10 people, 24 companies and 20 ships. Treasury's press release ties them to the shipping network of Mohammad Hossein Shamkhani, which it calls "a major force behind Iran's oil exports."

The release names Sea Lead Shipping PTE. Ltd. of Singapore and three of its subsidiaries. Sea Lead managed and operated three ships that OFAC lists as container ships. Treasury also says a We Freight group provided "transportation intermediary services" to the network's container shipping. A 2024 note from Treasury, Commerce and Justice explains that OFAC can fine a firm under US jurisdiction even if it did not know, or have reason to know, that a deal was prohibited.

sections.h2: The variants in OFAC's own documents
html:
• NUVETRRO or Nuvettro. The SDN List spells the owner of the ship JADE as NUVETRRO SHIPPING INC. The annex of General License Z spells it Nuvettro.
  • We Freight or WeFreight. Its SDN entry uses WE FREIGHT in three names and WEFREIGHT in one.
  • One brand for four companies. Each Sea Lead company has its own SDN entry, so a document that names only the brand does not say which one is meant.
  • Short ship names. In our test, OPAL, JADE and NADIA each returned another listed ship. The ship ELPINIKI also goes by "CORN," which OFAC marks as a weak alias. OFAC says such an alias "may generate a large volume of false hits."
  • A street that is also a ship. Sea Lead's listed address is 78 Shenton Way, Singapore, and OFAC links the ship SHENTON WAY to Sea Lead.
  • Names in other scripts. OFAC prints 15 of the new names in Arabic or Chinese script. None of them was in the copy of the SDN List our tool used for the test below, which OFAC published on October 5.

On October 7, 2026, we ran our tool, Crusetra Screening 0.1.0, on 103 names, against ten lists downloaded the day before. They were the listed names as OFAC prints them, the ships again with their IMO numbers, and 32 variants we wrote, one of them Sea Lead's address. We left out the 10 people, because the tool is built for companies and vessels.

Scores run from 0 to 1. At 0.81 or more the match is strong. From 0.80 to just under 0.81 it is possible, and the tool caps a match at 0.80 when it has a reason to doubt it. A person confirms or clears every match.
Each of the other 102 names should match a July 14 entry. The tool found the right one as a strong match for 96, as a possible match for 3, and missed 3.

What worked. Every company name, company alias and ship name typed as OFAC prints it scored 1.000 on the right entry. "Nuvettro Shipping Inc" scored 0.933, and both spellings of We Freight scored 1.000. Without its IMO number, OPAL returned two entries for another listed OPAL, both ranked above the right one, and NADIA returned the listed ship NADIYA. The IMO number removed both. A made-up ship name with SHENTON WAY's IMO number matched SHENTON WAY, and the tool treated our name as a new name for that ship.

What fell short. "SEALEAD" alone found none of the four Sea Lead entries. It showed four unrelated entries at 0.800, and a reviewer who cleared them would let the brand through. Both names we tried in Arabic script missed. Three names reached only 0.800, among them "TANJONG PAGAR" without its 1 and the alias "CORN."

Extra alerts. The address returned the ship SHENTON WAY as a possible match. That entry is wrong, but it still points to Sea Lead. Another 13 names brought up 30 entries from outside the July 14 listings, 26 of them possible matches, plus 5 the tool counted without showing. The IMO number removed the other ships but no company entries, so a person still has to clear those.

Ask for the IMO number of every vessel and screen it with the name. It is a permanent number that is never given to another ship, and in our test it told same-name ships apart. Ask for full legal names in Latin letters too. The tool missed the brand alone and the Arabic names, but it caught the same companies under their full legal names.

sections.h2: What this test does not show
html: These counts come from one day of OFAC listings, so they do not show how often the tool catches names in general. We wrote the variants knowing the listed names, and your files may hold forms we did not imagine. The tool compares names and IMO numbers only. It does not check ownership. A company owned 50 percent or more by blocked parties is blocked too, even when it is not on the SDN List.
This article reports one test of our tool. It is not legal advice. Read about the tool at crusetra.com/screening.
How we ran it: Crusetra Screening 0.1.0, commit a2a9633, offline, with CRUSETRA_OFFLINE=1 npm run cribler -- --names=<the file of 103 names>.
